titre: The man who coined “form follows function” never gave up ornament
accroche: Sullivan wrote the line that would justify all the bareness of the twentieth century, but his own towers disappear under terra-cotta plant motifs.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1891, architect Louis Sullivan delivers the Wainwright Building in St. Louis, ten stories of offices for brewer Ellis Wainwright. The structure is steel, but nothing about it is bare: a terra-cotta frieze of foliage runs beneath the cornice, different plant motifs adorn each story between the windows, and oculi framed by scrollwork punctuate the top level. This is the work of the man who, five years later, will write the most-quoted sentence in twentieth-century architecture, the one invoked today to justify stripping everything away.

## A law borrowed from the eagle and the apple tree

In March 1896, in Lippincott's Magazine, Sullivan publishes “The Tall Office Building Artistically Considered.” In it he looks for a rule of composition for a new kind of object, the steel-framed office building, by observing nature: whether it be the sweeping eagle in his flight, the open apple blossom, the toiling work horse, the blithe swan, the branching oak, the winding stream at its base, the drifting clouds, over all the coursing sun, form ever follows function, and this is the law. The formula will later be boiled down to four words: “form follows function.”

Sullivan is not describing a bare building. He proposes a composition in three parts: a commercial base for the ground-floor shop windows, a stack of identical floors for the offices, whose function does not change from one level to the next, and an attic story that closes off the whole, each part expressing its own function through its form. Nothing in the text rules out ornament. Sullivan made it his signature throughout his career, even developing a vocabulary of interlaced foliage that now bears his name, the Sullivanesque style, found in terra cotta on the facades he builds, including the Wainwright Building, completed five years before the essay was published.

## What this shifts

It is after Sullivan's death, in 1924, that his formula changes sides. The European modernists, carried by the slogan of Austrian architect Adolf Loos that ornament is a crime, take it up as historical endorsement for entirely smooth facades. A law meant to unite form and meaning becomes, decades later, the alibi for a bareness its author never practiced: the man who formulated it spent his career ornamenting what he built, and the bare glass towers that cite it ignore half of what it said.

carte.punch: “Form follows function” comes from an architect who never stopped carving foliage.
carte.idee: In 1896, Louis Sullivan writes that form ever follows function. He calls for no bareness: his own building, the Wainwright Building, is covered in ornamental terra cotta. It is the modernists, after his death, who turn his formula into an argument against ornament.

quiz.question: Why could twentieth-century modernists invoke “form follows function” to justify facades without ornament?
choix: Because Sullivan himself gave up ornament in the second half of his career, after the Wainwright Building
Because they kept the formula without the context in which Sullivan stated it, a context that does not rule out ornament
Because Sullivan had publicly supported Adolf Loos's slogan that ornament is a crime
Because the Wainwright Building, his best-known building, already had no decoration at all
quiz.explication: Sullivan formulated his law to describe a unity between form and function, never to ban ornament: he made it his signature throughout his career, including on the Wainwright Building. He neither gave up decoration nor supported Loos, whose slogan came after him and runs counter to his own practice.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Sullivan compose the steel-framed office building in his 1896 essay?
choix: In three parts: commercial base, stack of identical floors, final attic story
In only two parts, a massive base and a tapering top
In four parts, one for each facade of the building
With no fixed composition, left to each architect's freedom
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card details this three-part composition that Sullivan proposes: a commercial base for the shop windows, a stack of identical floors for the offices, and an attic story that closes off the whole, each part expressing its function through its form.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does Sullivan draw his rule that form ever follows function?
choix: From his own earlier building plans, compared with one another
From the treatises of ancient architecture he had studied in Paris
From nature: the soaring eagle, the apple blossom, the oak, the stream
From occupancy statistics of the office buildings of his day
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card quotes the 1896 essay in which Sullivan seeks this rule by observing nature, the sweeping eagle, the open apple blossom, the oak, the winding stream: form there ever follows function, and this is the law.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When and by whom does Sullivan's formula change sides, to justify facades without ornament?
choix: In his lifetime, when Sullivan himself gives up ornament
As early as 1896, the very year his essay is published
After 1950, when his heirs sell the rights to the formula
After his death in 1924, taken up by the modernists and Adolf Loos
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The card places this shift after Sullivan's death in 1924: the European modernists, carried by Adolf Loos's slogan that ornament is a crime, then take up his formula as historical endorsement.
